what: The topics, subtopics and actions every San Francisco Board of Supervisors record is classified into, 1906-2026.
why_three_columns: One column could not hold it. 'Appropriating $232,530, Water Department, reconstruction of Market Street water mains' is an appropriation (what the Board DID) about water (what it was ABOUT). Forcing both into one field made 'money set aside' swallow every record that mentioned a sum, and it was the single largest source of disagreement when the rule pass was checked against a hand-read sample. So: `topic` and `subtopic` say what it is about, `action` says what the Board did.
read_by: the rule pass, which no longer classifies and only CHECKS the classifier
counting: A record has exactly one topic, at most one subtopic, and exactly one action. No record is therefore counted under two topics — but the topics sum to the records that carry one, not to every record: a decision whose line names an act and no subject keeps an empty topic. Do not add topics to tags.

topics.label: The street
topics.note: The strip outside a front door, and what runs under it. The largest thing in the record for the first half of the century.

topics.label: Getting around
topics.note: Moving through the city, and the companies that were licensed to move people through it.

topics.label: Land and building
topics.note: Who may build what, and who owns the ground.

topics.label: Doing business
topics.note: The permit trade. For four decades this was the single commonest thing the Board did: licensing small industry one address at a time. It is 27% of the 1900s and 0% after 1940.

topics.label: What the city runs
topics.note: The buildings and services the city owns and operates.

topics.label: Running the city
topics.note: The Board acting on itself and on the machinery of government.

subtopics.label: A vote or a scheduling step

topics.label: Public money
topics.note: Only where money ITSELF is the subject. An appropriation FOR a park is a parks record whose action is `appropriated` — it does not belong here. This was the mistake that made an earlier version of this list unusable.

topics.label: Civic life
topics.note: The Board speaking rather than deciding.

subtopics.label: Positions on state and national matters

actions.label: Granted
actions.note: permission, a licence, a franchise, an extension of time

actions.label: Refused
actions.note: denied an application. Frequent in the early record and easy to miss — a denial reads almost exactly like a grant.

actions.label: Ordered
actions.note: directed that work be done, or that a thing happen

actions.label: Accepted
actions.note: accepted finished work, a deed, a gift, a report

actions.label: Set money aside
actions.note: for anything. The topic says what for.

actions.label: Paid
actions.note: a claim, a contractor, a refund

actions.label: Amended
actions.note: changed an existing rule, map or ordinance

actions.label: Commended or urged
actions.note: praised, proclaimed, or took a position

actions.label: Voted or scheduled
actions.note: adopted, continued, referred, tabled, second reading — the Board acting on its own calendar

record_types.label: A decision
record_types.note: a real record that says what it was about

record_types.label: A vote outcome only
record_types.note: the description is in another record

record_types.label: Page header or footer
record_types.note: ONLY when that is the whole record. A footer trailing a real decision does not make it furniture — that mistake called four real decisions furniture in testing.

record_types.label: Cut in half by a page break
Departmental report text
record_types.note: kind = W. Engineering annual reports, not Board acts. 0.9% of the corpus.

record_types.label: Public comment
record_types.note: What a member of the public said about a file, printed under the item they spoke to: "Resolution urging … (File No. 190118). Anuba S; expressed support." It is a record of the meeting, not an act of the Board, and it carries no topic of its own — the topic belongs to the file being spoken to, which has its own row.
